source: A companion workbook to the ideas in Alex Hormozi's book $100M Money Models (Acquisition.com, 2025). Every lesson here is a paraphrase in this app's own words, never the book's text; the exercises are the book's homework restated as things to type, tick or pick. Read the book for the reasoning and the stories. Play names are this app's plain-word labels for the book's offer types.
confidenceNote: Thresholds (pay back the cost of a customer in 30 days, twice that to self-fund, lifetime gross profit at least three times the cost of a customer) are the book's rules of thumb, not measured findings. Your own numbers decide.
note: Read by moneymodels/engines/model.js. Six planets, five bands of three levels each, 90 levels. A band means the same depth on every planet: Learn (read and check), Numbers (type your figures), Build (the exercises), Prove (run it and measure), Optimize (stack and sharpen). A recipe of tier N may need only facts from bands 1 to N (linted).

planets.label: Foundations
planets.blurb: What a money model is, what it costs you to get a customer today, and the one rule the whole book rests on.

planets.label: Attraction
planets.blurb: The first yes: the offer that turns a stranger into a customer without draining your cash.

planets.label: Upsell
planets.blurb: The bigger yes, asked at the moment it is easiest to say. Where the model makes its money.

planets.label: Downsell
planets.blurb: The smaller yes after a no. Keeps the customer and recovers cash you would have lost.

planets.label: Continuity
planets.blurb: The yes that repeats: getting customers to keep paying, which is what makes lifetime profit large.

planets.label: KPIs and Scale
planets.blurb: The six numbers to watch, the two thresholds, and how fast customer money can fund the next customer.

bands.meaning: Read the idea, then answer one check question

bands.name: Numbers
bands.meaning: Type your figures for this part of the model

bands.name: Build
bands.meaning: The exercises: pick a play, write the offer, tick the design list

levels.title: What a money model is
lesson: A money model is a deliberate sequence of offers. Not one product with a price on it: the order in which you ask a customer to say yes, what you ask for each time, and what you do when they say no.
The point of the sequence is cash timing. A business that makes plenty of profit over two years can still die in month two, because the money to get the next customer is not back in the bank yet.
So the question the whole book asks is: how do you get a customer to pay you more, sooner, than it costs you to get and serve them?

quiz.q: Which of these is a money model?
options: A product with a good price
A sequence of offers: the first yes, a bigger yes, a smaller yes after a no, and a repeating yes
quiz.why: One price is one offer. A money model is the order of offers around it and what each one is for.

levels.title: The cash constraint and the 30-day rule
lesson: Every customer costs money to get (ads, time, commissions) and money to serve. If that cash comes back in a year, you can only afford as many customers as your savings allow. Growth is capped by your bank balance, not by demand.

The rule of thumb the book builds on: get back at least what a customer cost you within 30 days. Get back twice that and every customer pays for the next one. Then growth is funded by customers, not by you or a lender.
Thirty days is not magic. It is roughly how long a card bill or an ad invoice gives you before the money is due.

quiz.q: A customer costs $150 to get. What does the model want back from them inside 30 days?
options: At least $150, and ideally $300 or more
Whatever they pay over their lifetime
Nothing, as long as the business is profitable by year end
quiz.why: Break-even inside 30 days keeps you alive. Twice the cost lets the next customer be bought with this one's money.

levels.title: The four kinds of offer
lesson: Attraction offers get the first yes from a stranger. Their job is to bring people in cheaply, not to make the money.
Upsell offers ask for a bigger yes right after the first one, when trust is highest. This is where the model earns.
Downsell offers turn a no into a smaller yes: same promise, lighter package or easier terms.
Continuity offers get the customer to keep paying: a membership, a subscription, a retainer. This is what makes the lifetime value large.
Each of the next four planets takes one of these. Do them in order: a great upsell with no one to offer it to is worth nothing.

quiz.q: A customer says no to the bigger package. Which offer comes next?
options: A downsell: the same promise in a lighter or easier form
quiz.why: A no to the price or the size is not a no to the result. The downsell keeps the customer and some of the cash.

levels.title: What your main offer sells for today
lesson: Start with the business as it is. One product or service, the one most customers buy first. Its price, before any discount.

fields.label: Price of your main offer today
fields.help: What one customer pays for it. If it is monthly, use one month here; the model will handle the repeat part on the Continuity planet.

levels.title: What it costs you to deliver one
lesson: Everything you spend to serve one customer for that offer: materials, shipping, contractor hours, software seats, the hours you pay someone for. Not rent, not ads. If you deliver it yourself, count your hours at what you would pay someone else.

fields.label: Cost to deliver one sale
fields.help: Only the costs that happen because this one customer bought. Type 0 if there truly are none (a digital file, say).

levels.title: What a customer costs you to get
lesson: The cost of a customer is everything you spent to get customers in a month, divided by the customers you got. Ads, the person who runs them, referral fees, the free sessions you gave away. Last month is fine. A rough month is better than nothing; you will replace it on the Prove band.

fields.label: Spent on getting customers last month
fields.help: Ads, agency, commissions, giveaways, the salary of whoever does the marketing.

fields.label: New customers last month
fields.help: People who paid for the first time. Not leads, not sign-ups.

levels.title: Exercise: the promise in one line
lesson: Every offer in the model points at the same result. Write it the way the customer would say it, not the way your industry does. 'Lose the first ten pounds in six weeks' beats 'a holistic fitness programme'.
This line is reused on every planet: the attraction offer promises it, the upsell gets it faster, the downsell gets it lighter, continuity keeps it.

fields.label: Who the customer is, in a few words
fields.help: One kind of person. 'Busy parents who stopped exercising' is a customer; 'anyone' is not.

fields.label: The result they want, in their words
fields.help: A result with a size and a time if you can: what, how much, by when.

levels.title: Exercise: name the constraint
lesson: A business is held back by one thing at a time. Pick the one that is true right now. The model's planets map onto it: not enough customers is an attraction problem; not enough per customer is upsell and downsell; they do not stay is continuity; it costs too much to serve is a margin problem to fix before any of them.

fields.label: What is holding the business back right now?

options.label: Each customer does not pay enough
They do not stay or come back
It costs too much to serve them

levels.title: Exercise: map today's sequence
lesson: Write down what a customer is actually offered today, in the order it happens. Most businesses find they have one offer and then silence. That silence is the money model you are about to build.

fields.label: The first thing a stranger is offered
fields.help: The ad, the free consult, the intro price. Whatever comes first.

fields.label: What they are offered after buying
fields.help: Type 'nothing' if nothing. That is an honest and common answer.

fields.label: What happens when they say no
fields.help: A follow-up? A cheaper option? Nothing?

fields.label: What they pay for on an ongoing basis
fields.help: A membership, a retainer, refills, or 'nothing'.

levels.title: How long cash takes to come back today
lesson: From the day you spend the first dollar on getting a customer to the day their money is in your account. Count the sales cycle, the free trial, the invoice terms. This is the number the model shortens.

fields.label: Days from first ad dollar to first cash collected
fields.help: Typical, not best case. If you invoice on 30-day terms after a two-week trial, that is about 45.

levels.title: Cash per customer in their first 30 days, today
lesson: Take last month's new customers and add up everything they paid you in their first 30 days. Divide by how many there were. This is the before picture; the model page shows the after beside it.

fields.label: Cash collected per new customer in their first 30 days
fields.help: Collected, not invoiced. A payment plan counts only the payments that landed inside 30 days.

levels.title: Checklist: the numbers audit
lesson: Before building anything new, make sure the four foundation figures are real rather than remembered. Tick each once it comes from a statement, a report or a count, not a guess.

items.text: Marketing spend is tracked by channel, month by month
New customers are counted with where they came from
The cost to deliver one sale comes from real invoices or hours
The 30-day cash per customer was counted from actual payments
The constraint is written down where the team can see it

levels.title: Your hours per customer
lesson: The cost to deliver (level 5) priced your time at what you would pay someone else. This asks for the hours themselves: everything you personally spend on one customer in their first month, selling and serving. The model turns it into gross profit per hour of your time, which is the number that says whether to raise the price, cut delivery, or hire.

fields.label: Hours of your own time per customer, first month
fields.help: Selling, onboarding, delivering, chasing. A rough count is fine.

levels.title: Exercise: the play you run first
lesson: The constraint you named on level 8 says which planet to build first. Pick it here so the next-up card points at it. You can change your mind later; you cannot build four things at once.

fields.label: Which part of the model do you build first?

options.label: Upsell: earn more from each one
Downsell: lose fewer at the no

levels.title: Checklist: the weekly rhythm
lesson: The model is not a launch, it is a habit. Once a week, four numbers and one change.

items.text: Cost of a customer refreshed for last week
30-day cash per customer refreshed
The 30-day ratio compared with the two thresholds
One change chosen for next week, and only one

levels.title: What an attraction offer is for
lesson: The attraction offer's job is to turn a stranger into a customer. It is the door, not the room. If it makes a profit on its own, wonderful; if it only covers the cost of getting the customer, that is still a win, because the upsell and continuity are waiting behind it.
The mistake is to make the attraction offer the whole business: then every customer must be profitable on day one, and the price has to be high, and fewer people walk through the door.
A good attraction offer is easy to say yes to, makes the promise from Foundations level 7 in a small, fast form, and naturally leads to the next offer.

quiz.q: The attraction offer breaks even after covering the cost of the customer. Good or bad?
options: Bad: every offer should make a profit
Good: the customer cost nothing net, and the upsell and continuity are still to come
Neither, it depends on the industry
quiz.why: A free customer who then sees an upsell and a continuity offer is the whole idea.

levels.title: The attraction plays
lesson: Win your money back: the customer pays, and gets it back (or as credit) if they hit a defined result and follow the rules. Most will not hit it; the ones who do are the ones you want to keep.
Giveaway: one big prize, many entrants, and everyone who did not win gets an offer. Cheap leads at volume.
Decoy: a free or very cheap option beside the real one, so the real one looks like the sensible choice, and the free option filters out people who would never pay.
Buy some, get some free: bundle volume up front. The free part is margin you would have spent on getting them back anyway.
Pay less now or pay more later: two prices for the same thing, a smaller one paid today and a larger one paid on results or over time. Both close; one brings cash forward.
Free with strings: free only when the string (a deposit, a booked call, an upsell moment) makes the free customer pay off.

quiz.q: In 'win your money back', who ends up refunded?
options: The few who hit the stated result and followed every rule
quiz.why: The condition is real and reachable. The people who reach it are your best customers, and the refund is cheaper than the ad that would have found them.

levels.title: The three parts every attraction offer needs
lesson: A clear result with a time on it. Not 'a great experience'; 'ten pounds in six weeks'.
A reason it is cheap or free that the customer believes: a challenge, a first-time price, a limited batch, a prize. Cheap with no reason reads as low quality.
A string that leads to the next offer: the results call, the check-in, the thing they have to come in for. That is where the upsell lives.

quiz.q: Which attraction offer is missing something?
options: 'Six-week challenge, $500, win it back if you finish all 18 sessions'
'Free strategy session, then we build your plan together'
quiz.why: A discount has no result, no reason and no string. The other two have all three.

levels.title: The attraction offer's price
lesson: What the stranger pays for the first yes. Type 0 if the plan is free with strings; that is a real answer and the model will treat it as one.

fields.label: Price of the attraction offer
fields.help: The cash collected up front, before any refund or credit.

levels.title: What the attraction offer costs to deliver
lesson: Same idea as Foundations level 5, for this offer. Include the prize if it is a giveaway (prize cost divided by expected entrants) and the expected refunds if it is win-your-money-back (Prove level 11 sharpens that).

fields.label: Cost to deliver the attraction offer to one customer
fields.help: Per customer, all in. 0 is allowed.

levels.title: Leads, and how many of them buy
lesson: A lead is someone who raised a hand: a form, a call, a walk-in. The share who take the attraction offer is the conversion rate. Together with what you spend (Foundations 6) this gives the cost of a lead.

fields.label: Leads per month
fields.help: People who asked, booked or messaged. Last month is fine.

fields.label: Share of leads who take the attraction offer
fields.help: Buyers divided by leads, as a percent.

levels.title: Exercise: pick your attraction play
lesson: The Plays page says which of these the numbers already support for you. Pick one. A second one comes on the Optimize band.

fields.label: Your attraction play

options.label: Pay less now or pay more later

levels.title: Exercise: write the offer in one sentence
lesson: Use the frame: 'Get [the result] in [the time] for [the price], and [the reason it is cheap or the condition of the reward].' Then add the string: what happens next that leads to the upsell.
Say it out loud. If it takes two breaths, it is too long.

fields.label: The attraction offer, one sentence
fields.help: Result, time, price, reason.

fields.label: The string: what leads to the next offer
fields.help: The results call, the week-two check-in, the pickup, the delivery.

levels.title: Checklist: attraction offer design
lesson: Tick what the offer as written has. Anything unticked is the next thing to fix before it goes out.

items.text: Names one result with a size and a time
Gives a believable reason it is cheap or free
Has a deadline or a limited number
Has a string that puts the customer in front of the upsell
Any money-back or reward has a measurable, written condition
The price covers the cost to deliver it
You can count who came in through it

levels.title: How many buyers actually show up
lesson: A customer who paid and never came in cannot be upsold. Show rate is the share of attraction buyers who consume the thing (attend, open, start). The upsell take rate on the next planet is measured on these people.

fields.label: Share of attraction buyers who show up or start
fields.help: From your first run. 100 if everyone did.

levels.title: What you actually paid back
lesson: For win-your-money-back and any guarantee: the share of buyers who got a refund or credit. Type 0 if the play has no refund. This sharpens the attraction offer's real margin.

fields.label: Share of attraction buyers refunded or credited
fields.help: Refunds paid divided by buyers. 0 if none.

levels.title: Checklist: the first test run
lesson: One channel, one offer, one week. The point is to count, not to win.

items.text: Ran on one channel only, so the count is clean
Ran for a fixed period with a real deadline
Counted leads
Counted buyers
Counted every dollar spent, including time
Wrote down the top three reasons people said no

levels.title: Exercise: stack a second play
lesson: Plays combine. A giveaway feeds a decoy (the losers get the cheap option beside the real one). Win-your-money-back stacks on a challenge. Pick the second play that feeds the first.

fields.label: The second attraction play

options.label: Pay less now or pay more later

levels.title: The limit that makes the deadline real
lesson: Scarcity only works when it is true. Decide how many you will take per run (seats, units, slots) and say it. When it sells out, it sells out.

fields.label: Customers you will take per run
fields.help: A number you would actually stop at.

levels.title: Checklist: sharpening the attraction offer
lesson: Change one thing per run, in this order. Each tick is one run.

items.text: Made the promise bigger or more specific
Shortened the deadline or lowered the cap
Added a bonus that costs you little and them a lot to get elsewhere
Tested a second price point
Cut the cost to deliver without cutting the result

levels.title: Why the moment after a yes is worth the most
lesson: Someone who just paid you trusts you more than they will at any other point. They have decided you are worth money. Asking for a bigger yes in that window is far cheaper than finding a new customer.
The upsell is where the money model makes its money. The attraction offer pays for the customer; the upsell pays for the business.
The rule: the upsell must be a faster, bigger or easier way to get the same result they just bought. Not a different product. 'You want this; this gets you there sooner.'

quiz.q: When is the upsell cheapest to make?
options: A month after the first purchase, once they have seen results
Right after the first yes, or right after their first win
Before they buy anything, to anchor high
quiz.why: Trust peaks at the yes and at the first result. Both are upsell moments; the first is the one most businesses skip.

levels.title: The upsell plays
lesson: Classic: the next thing they need to get the result faster or keep it. The membership after the challenge, the installation after the product.
Menu: several add-ons, they pick. People say yes to something more often than to one thing.
Anchor: show the biggest option first. The one you actually want to sell looks reasonable next to it.
Rollover: credit what they just paid toward the bigger thing. 'The $500 you paid comes off the $2,000 programme.' The first purchase becomes a deposit.

quiz.q: What does a rollover upsell do with the money the customer already paid?
options: Counts it toward the bigger offer, so the first purchase becomes a deposit
quiz.why: A customer who has already paid part of the bigger thing is halfway to yes.

levels.title: The ask
lesson: An upsell that is never offered has a take rate of zero. Most upsell problems are not the offer; it is that nobody asked.
Ask in one sentence, as a service: 'Since you want [result], the people who get there fastest also [next step]. Want me to add it?' Then stop talking.
Every customer is asked. Not the ones who look rich. Every one.

quiz.q: The upsell take rate is 5%. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether every customer was actually offered it
quiz.why: Offered-to share times take-rate-when-offered is the real number. Fix the asking before the offer.

levels.title: The upsell's price
lesson: The bigger yes. If it is a payment plan, type the total here; the Downsell planet handles split terms.

fields.label: Price of the upsell
fields.help: Total price, before any rollover credit.

levels.title: What the upsell costs to deliver
lesson: Per customer, all in, for the whole thing you are selling.

fields.label: Cost to deliver the upsell to one customer
fields.help: Materials, hours, seats. 0 is allowed.

levels.title: How many take it
lesson: Of the customers offered the upsell, the share who say yes. If you have not run it yet, use a modest guess (one in five is a common starting point for a well-matched upsell) and mark it to revisit on Prove.

fields.label: Share of customers offered the upsell who take it
fields.help: Takers divided by those asked, as a percent.

levels.title: Exercise: pick your upsell play
lesson: Classic if there is an obvious next step. Menu if you have several. Anchor if you have a premium tier. Rollover if the attraction offer's price is a meaningful part of the upsell's.

fields.label: Your upsell play

options.label: Rollover: first payment becomes a deposit

levels.title: Exercise: write the upsell script
lesson: One sentence to ask, one sentence for the most common no. The frame: 'Since you want [result], most people who get it fastest also [next step]. Want me to add that?'

fields.label: The ask, in one sentence
fields.help: Say it as a service, not a sale.

fields.label: What you say to the most common no
fields.help: Usually it leads to the downsell.

levels.title: Checklist: upsell design
lesson: Tick what is true of the upsell as written.

items.text: Offered within minutes of the first yes, or at the first win
Gets the same result faster, bigger or easier
Priced above the attraction offer
Cost to deliver is known
The ask fits in one sentence
A no does not undo the first sale
There is a way to make sure every customer is asked

levels.title: When it is offered
lesson: Days after the first purchase. Day 0 is at the checkout. This decides whether the upsell's cash lands inside the 30 days.

fields.label: Days after the first purchase the upsell is offered
fields.help: 0 if at checkout. 14 if at the two-week check-in.

levels.title: How many were actually asked
lesson: From the first run: of the customers who showed up, the share who were offered the upsell at all. This is the number that is usually the problem.

fields.label: Share of customers who were offered the upsell
fields.help: Asked divided by customers who showed up.

levels.title: Checklist: the first upsell run
lesson: Two weeks of asking every customer, counting, and listening.

items.text: The script was used word for word
Every customer was asked (a tally proves it)
Counted asked and took
Heard and wrote down the top reason for no
Changed one thing for the next run

levels.title: A second upsell
lesson: After the first upsell, a second one to the people who took it: the done-with-you tier, the equipment, the extra seats. Price and expected take.

fields.label: Price of the second upsell
fields.help: Offered to takers of the first.

fields.label: Share of first-upsell takers who take it
fields.help: A guess is fine to start.

levels.title: The anchor price
lesson: The biggest thing you could sell, priced as if someone will buy it. Some will. The rest see the real upsell as reasonable.

fields.label: Price of your top tier
fields.help: Shown first, sold rarely.

levels.title: Checklist: sharpening the upsell
lesson: One per run.

items.text: Showed the anchor before the real upsell
Turned one upsell into a short menu
Credited the first payment toward the upsell
Raised the price 10% and watched the take rate
Added a second ask at the customer's first win

levels.title: A no is not the end
lesson: When a customer says no to the upsell, most businesses stop. The customer wanted the result a minute ago; what they said no to was the size or the terms.

A downsell offers a smaller yes: the same promise with less in the box, or the same box with easier terms. It recovers cash that was walking out, and it keeps the customer in the sequence for continuity.
Order matters: first change the terms (a payment plan), then the package (a lighter version), then the price. Cutting the price first teaches customers to say no.

quiz.q: The customer says no to a $2,000 programme. What is the first downsell to try?
options: The same programme at $2,000 in four payments
quiz.why: Same value, easier terms. Price cuts come last and cost the most.

levels.title: The downsell plays
lesson: Payment plan: the same offer split over time. Usually the first thing to try, and often the only one needed.
Trial with a string: try it, and pay if you keep it, or pay a penalty if you do not do the work. The string keeps the free part from being free forever.
Lighter version: fewer parts, less access, less support, same result more slowly. Keep the promise, shrink the package.
Deposit and decide: a small payment to hold the price or the spot, decided later. Cash today, and a reason to come back.

quiz.q: What makes a trial a downsell rather than a giveaway?
options: There is a string: a payment if they keep it or do not do the work
It is only for some people
quiz.why: A trial with no string is a free customer with no path to paying. The string is the point.

levels.title: Where the downsell sits
lesson: There are two nos in the model. The no to the attraction offer (a stranger who did not buy) and the no to the upsell (a customer who did not go bigger). Each can have a downsell.
Start with the second. Those people already paid you once, showed up, and heard the upsell. A smaller yes from them is the easiest cash in the business.
The downsell after the attraction offer comes on the Optimize band, once the rest works.

quiz.q: Which downsell should be built first?
options: The one for strangers who did not buy the attraction offer
The one for customers who said no to the upsell
quiz.why: They are warm, present and have already paid. Build where the yes is easiest.

levels.title: The downsell's price
lesson: What the smaller yes costs the customer in total. For a payment plan on the same upsell, that may equal the upsell price; the terms are what changed.

fields.label: Price of the downsell
fields.help: Total over all payments.

levels.title: What the downsell costs to deliver
lesson: Per customer. A lighter version should cost less to deliver; a payment plan costs the same as the upsell.

fields.label: Cost to deliver the downsell to one customer
fields.help: All in. 0 is allowed.

levels.title: How many take it
lesson: Of the customers who said no to the upsell and were offered the downsell, the share who take it.

fields.label: Share of upsell nos who take the downsell
fields.help: Takers divided by those offered, as a percent.

levels.title: Exercise: pick your downsell play
lesson: Payment plan unless there is a clear reason not to. The Plays page says which ones the numbers support.

fields.label: Your downsell play

levels.title: Exercise: write the downsell script
lesson: It follows the no directly. 'Totally fair. Would it help if we did [terms or lighter version] instead? You would still get [result], just [the change].'

fields.label: The downsell, in one sentence
fields.help: Acknowledge the no, offer the smaller yes, keep the result.

fields.label: What exactly is smaller
fields.help: Fewer sessions, longer terms, less support, no guarantee. Name it.

levels.title: Checklist: downsell design
lesson: Tick what is true of the downsell as written.

items.text: Keeps the same result, only the package or terms shrink
Terms were tried before price
Still covers its cost to deliver
Still puts the customer in front of the continuity offer
Is never advertised, only offered after a no
The offer fits in one sentence

levels.title: The payment plan's shape
lesson: How many payments, and how big the first one is. The first payment is what lands inside the 30 days; the rest is a promise.

fields.label: Number of payments
fields.help: 1 if paid in full.

fields.label: Share of the price paid up front
fields.help: The first payment as a percent of the total. 100 if paid in full.

levels.title: How many plans fail
lesson: Payment plans leak. The share of plan customers who stop paying before the end. Type 0 if none have.

fields.label: Share of payment plans that stop early
fields.help: Stopped divided by started.

levels.title: Checklist: the first downsell run
lesson: Two weeks, every no gets the downsell, count what happens.

items.text: Every upsell no was offered the downsell
Counted offered and took
Payment plans are tracked to the last payment
Wrote down why people said no to the downsell too
Changed one thing for the next run

levels.title: A downsell for the first no
lesson: For strangers who did not take the attraction offer: a lower entry. A single session, a smaller batch, a deposit. Price and expected take among those who said no.

fields.label: Price of the entry downsell
fields.help: Offered to leads who did not buy the attraction offer.

fields.label: Share of attraction nos who take it
fields.help: A guess is fine to start.

levels.title: Exercise: the second thing you can shrink
lesson: If the first downsell is a payment plan, the second is a lighter version, and the other way round. Pick what you cut in the second one.

fields.label: What the second downsell cuts

levels.title: Checklist: sharpening the downsell
lesson: One per run.

items.text: Raised the first payment's share
Cut the number of payments
Put every plan on automatic payment
Added the second downsell after the second no
Tested a deposit-and-decide for the walkaways

levels.title: One sale into many
lesson: A customer who pays once is a transaction. A customer who pays every month is an asset. Continuity is what turns the model from a series of launches into a business that grows while you sleep.
The lifetime gross profit of a customer is mostly continuity. A $150 a month membership with 8% monthly churn is worth about twelve and a half months, over $1,800 of revenue, from one yes.
Every earlier offer should end by placing the customer in front of the continuity offer.

quiz.q: Monthly churn is 10%. On average how many months does a member stay?
quiz.why: Expected months is one divided by the monthly churn: 1 / 0.10 = 10.

levels.title: The continuity plays
lesson: Bonus for committing: a gift, worth a lot to them and little to you, for joining the ongoing plan today.
Discount for a longer term: pay for a year, get it cheaper. Cash forward, churn removed.
Waived fee: the setup or first month is free if they join now. The fee exists so that waiving it means something.
Bonuses over time: something new arrives in month two, month three, month six. Reasons to stay, not just reasons to join.
The default: the ongoing plan is the normal thing to buy; the one-off is the exception you have to ask for.

options: Getting people to stay, by giving them something to wait for
quiz.why: Joining bonuses fight the first no. Bonuses over time fight churn.

levels.title: Churn is the tax
lesson: Churn is the share of members who leave each month. Halving it doubles the value of every customer you already have, without a single new lead.
Measure it monthly, by cohort (people who joined the same month). A single average hides a leak in month two.
Most churn happens early, before the customer has had a win. The continuity offer's first job is to get them a win fast.

quiz.q: Churn drops from 10% to 5% a month. What happens to the average member's lifetime value?
quiz.why: Expected months goes from 10 to 20. Same price, twice the months.

levels.title: The six numbers
lesson: Cost of a customer (CAC): what you spend to get one.
Gross profit per sale: price minus the cost to deliver.
30-day cash: gross profit collected from a customer in their first 30 days, across the whole sequence.
Lifetime gross profit (LTGP): everything a customer earns you, less delivery, over their whole stay.
LTGP to CAC: how many times over a customer pays for themselves.
Payback days: how long until a customer has paid back their cost.

quiz.q: Price $500, cost to deliver $120, cost of the customer $150. What is the gross profit per sale?
quiz.why: Gross profit is price minus delivery cost: 500 minus 120. The cost of the customer is compared against it, not subtracted from it.

levels.title: The two thresholds
lesson: 30-day cash at least equal to CAC: you break even on each customer before the bills for getting them are due. You are alive.
30-day cash at least twice CAC: each customer funds the next one. You can grow as fast as you can deliver, with no outside money.
LTGP at least three times CAC: the business is worth running. Below that, the customers are barely paying for the marketing.

quiz.q: 30-day cash is $300 and CAC is $150. Which is true?
options: Self-funding: each customer pays for the next
quiz.why: Twice the cost inside 30 days is the self-funding line.

levels.title: The four ways to grow
lesson: More customers (attraction). More per customer (upsell, downsell, price). More often (continuity). Less to deliver (margin).
Every business grows through those four, and only those four. When you are stuck, the constraint from Foundations level 8 names which one.
The model's charts move when you move any of them; try it on the Model page once your numbers are in.

quiz.q: Which of these is not one of the four ways to grow?
options: Each sale costs less to deliver
quiz.why: An office is a cost. Growth comes from customers, price, frequency and margin.

levels.title: How many you can serve
lesson: The ceiling on the other side: customers you can take on in a month before quality drops. The growth chart flattens here.

fields.label: Most new customers you can serve in a month
fields.help: Honest, at current staff and hours.

levels.title: What the business costs to keep open
lesson: Rent, salaries, software, insurance: the monthly costs that do not change with one more customer. Gross profit has to cover this before there is any profit.

fields.label: Fixed costs per month
fields.help: Everything that is due whether or not a customer buys.

levels.title: The loop: cash in, share back in
lesson: Two figures that decide how fast the model can spin. The cash you can put toward getting customers each month is the ceiling before the model self-funds. The share of each month's 30-day cash you put back into ads is what makes the ceiling rise. 100 is all of it.

fields.label: Cash available for getting customers each month
fields.help: What you could spend on ads and sales this month without missing payroll or rent.

fields.label: Share of 30-day cash reinvested in getting customers
fields.help: As a percent. 50 is half.
